name: Amritsar
tagline: Spiritual heart of the Sikhs around the Golden Temple.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: Cool, clear winters from October to March are best, with Baisakhi in April and Gurpurab in November lighting the Golden Temple. Avoid the searing summer.

ourTake.lede: Amritsar is essentially about two things done exceptionally well: the Golden Temple and the food. See the temple at both night and dawn, when it is quietest and most moving, and eat your way through the old city rather than the hotel restaurants. The Wagah border ceremony is a spectacle but heavily touristy; go if it interests you, but the temple and the Partition Museum are the deeper experiences.
ourTake.comeIf: You want the Golden Temple at first light and the finest Punjabi food there is.
ourTake.skipIf: You want beaches, nightlife or a long stay.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

credentials: Taj Hotels flagship five-star in Amritsar
157 rooms and suites; J Wellness Circle spa
items.description: The city's flagship five-star, Taj polish and Punjabi warmth, five kilometres from the Golden Temple.

items.name: Hyatt Regency Amritsar Hotel & Spa
credentials: Hyatt Regency five-star deluxe
Shanti Spa, the largest spa in Amritsar
Complimentary Golden Temple coach transfers

items.name: Radisson Blu Hotel, Amritsar
credentials: Radisson Blu five-star
Largest ballroom in Amritsar; two lawns
Complimentary Golden Temple shuttle
items.description: A grounds-set Radisson Blu with the largest ballroom in the city, the wedding address on the airport road.

items.name: Ranjit's SVAASA
credentials: WelcomHeritage heritage boutique haveli
TripAdvisor Certificate / Award of Excellence (repeat)
Award-winning Hibiscus Pavilion spa
items.description: A 200-year-old family haveli reborn as a wellness boutique, the only true heritage stay in Amritsar.

items.name: Holiday Inn Amritsar Ranjit Avenue
credentials: IHG Holiday Inn, international mid-luxury standard
items.description: A dependable IHG house in the leafy Ranjit Avenue district, well-run and central to the newer city.

items.name: Sri Harmandir Sahib (The Golden Temple)
items.description: The gilded sanctum floats at the centre of the Amrit Sarovar, its reflection breaking gently on the water while unbroken kirtan drifts across the marble. For a Sikh-heritage family it is the still point of the whole journey; for anyone it is one of the most moving spaces in India.

items.name: The Parikrama
items.description: The white marble walkway that rings the sarovar, walked barefoot and clockwise, past pilgrims, gilt-edged shrines and the slow ripple of the tank. A private guide who knows where to pause turns a circuit into a reading of five centuries of Sikh history.

items.name: The Akal Takht
items.description: The seat of temporal Sikh authority, facing the Harmandir Sahib across the causeway, where the community's edicts have been issued since 1606. Standing before it explains the Sikh idea that the spiritual and the political are one.

items.name: The Amrit Sarovar (Holy Tank)
items.description: The pool of nectar that gives Amritsar its name, its steps worn smooth by generations who bathe here at dawn. Sitting at the water's edge in the quiet before sunrise is the single most peaceful hour the city offers.

items.name: The Palki Sahib Ceremony (Night)
items.description: Each night the Guru Granth Sahib is carried on a silver-and-gold palanquin from the sanctum to the Akal Takht amid rosewater and shouldered devotion, the Sukhasan ritual ending around 9:30-10 PM. Attending it, then again the Prakash before dawn, bookends a stay in something unforgettable.

items.name: Dawn Darshan & The Prakash Ceremony
items.description: In the dark small hours the Guru Granth Sahib is installed in the sanctum and the first hymns rise as the sky lightens over the gold. Arriving at 3-4 AM with a guide who can move you through the crowd is a rare, unhurried privilege.

items.name: The Langar (Guru Ka Langar)
items.description: The world's largest free community kitchen feeds up to a hundred thousand people a day, everyone seated on the floor as equals. Rolling rotis alongside the sevadars for an hour is a humbling, hands-on experience that stays with multi-generational travellers.

items.name: Central Sikh Museum
items.description: Above the main entrance to the complex, galleries of Guru portraits, martyr paintings, arms and rare manuscripts trace the faith's history and its long line of sacrifice. A quiet, weighty counterpoint to the devotion outside, and free to enter.

items.name: Gurdwara Baba Atal Rai
items.description: A nine-storey octagonal tower beside the Golden Temple, its walls once painted with frescoes of Guru Nanak's life, built in memory of Guru Hargobind's young son. Fewer visitors climb it, and the rooftop gives a rare high view over the sanctum and the old city.

items.name: Jallianwala Bagh
items.description: The walled garden where, in 1919, General Dyer's troops fired on a peaceful gathering; the bullet-marked wall and the martyrs' well remain, now within a renovated memorial complex with galleries and a light-and-sound show. A short walk from the Golden Temple and essential to understanding modern India.

items.name: Partition Museum
items.description: Housed in the restored colonial Town Hall, this is the world's first museum dedicated to the 1947 Partition, told through survivor testimony, personal objects and letters. For Punjabi families whose grandparents crossed the new border, it is often the most personal stop in the city.

items.name: Attari-Wagah Border Beating Retreat
items.description: The daily lowering-of-the-flags ceremony where Indian and Pakistani guards high-kick and posture as the crowd roars, held at the last checkpost before Lahore around 6 PM. Reserve VIP seating near the gate; the patriotism is unabashed and children love it.

items.name: Gobindgarh Fort
items.description: Maharaja Ranjit Singh's military fort, once the treasury of the Koh-i-Noor, reopened as a living-history complex with the Sher-e-Punjab 7D show, the Toshakhana turban museum, artisans and folk performers. A full evening's outing that works well across three generations.

items.name: Kandha Boldiyan Ne (Whispering Walls) Show
items.description: The nightly sound-and-light spectacle projected onto the fort's ramparts, telling the story of the fort and Ranjit Singh's Sikh empire after dark. Book the 8 PM show and pair it with an early dinner inside the fort's dhaba court.

items.name: Durgiana Temple
items.description: A Hindu temple to Durga and Lakshmi built in the 1920s in the very image of the Golden Temple, gilded and set in its own tank. It gives a fuller sense of Amritsar as a shared sacred city, and is far quieter than its famous cousin.

items.name: Ram Tirath Temple
items.description: The reputed hermitage of sage Valmiki, where legend places the birth of Luv and Kush and the writing of the Ramayana, marked by an ancient tank and a colossal Valmiki statue. A peaceful, mythic day-side detour that most tourists miss entirely.

items.name: Maharaja Ranjit Singh Museum & Summer Palace
items.description: The Lion of Punjab's own summer palace, set in the Ram Bagh gardens, now displaying his arms, armour, coins, miniatures and a panorama of the Sikh court. The best single place to meet the man whose empire made Amritsar, and to walk his gardens after.

items.name: Ram Bagh Garden (Company Bagh)
items.description: The formal garden Ranjit Singh laid out on the model of Lahore's Shalimar, with pavilions, a summer palace and old shade trees in the heart of the city. A cool, green interval between the intensity of the shrines.

items.name: Amritsar Heritage Walk (Old City)
items.description: A guided route through the 400-year-old walled city, from the Town Hall through the katras and akharas to the Golden Temple, past frescoed havelis, the old mint and hidden shrines. A private early-morning walk, before the crowds, is the finest way to read the real Amritsar.

items.name: Chitta Akhara
items.description: A monastic complex from 1781 on the heritage walk, prized for its delicate Rajasthani-influenced wall paintings tucked deep in the lanes. The kind of place only a good local guide will open for you.

items.name: Thathera Bazaar (Guru Bazaar Coppersmiths)
credentials: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage (Thatheras of Jandiala Guru)
items.description: The craft of the Thatheras, hand-beating brass and copper utensils in a rhythm unchanged for generations, is inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list. Watching a vessel take shape and taking one home is a genuinely rooted keepsake.

items.name: Kesar Da Dhaba
items.description: Serving since 1916 in a narrow old-city lane, famous for dal makhani slow-cooked overnight in a brass pot over wood flame, lachha parathas and firni. The unshowy, definitive Amritsari meal; a guide can arrange a quiet table away from the queue.

items.name: Bharawan Da Dhaba
items.description: A pre-Partition institution (since 1912) near the Town Hall, turning out tandoor-fresh kulchas, dahi bhalla and chole for the better part of a century. Vegetarian, generous and a fixture of any Amritsari food pilgrimage.

items.name: Amritsari Kulcha (The Dish)
items.description: The city's signature: a potato-and-spice-stuffed flatbread crisped in a tandoor, cracked open with white butter and dark chole. Worth eating at more than one address, kulcha crawl style, to argue over who does it best.

items.name: Ahuja Milk Bhandar (The Lassi)
items.description: The legendary spoon-thick lassi, so dense with malai you scoop rather than sip, poured in a cramped old-city corner. A five-minute detour that becomes a highlight; a private car and guide make the narrow lanes easy.

items.name: Kulcha Land
items.description: A cleaner, sit-down alternative to the old-city dhabas on the newer Lawrence Road, doing crisp stuffed kulchas washed down with lassi. Useful when travelling with elders who want the flavour without the crush.

items.name: Sadda Pind
items.description: A twelve-acre recreation of a 19th-century Punjabi village, with mud homes, artisans, Gatka, Bhangra, bioscope and a full Punjabi buffet. A curated, comfortable way to give children and grandparents the rural Punjab their family came from; overnight stays exist for the fully immersed.

items.name: Khalsa College
items.description: A 300-acre campus of magnificent Indo-Saracenic architecture designed by Bhai Ram Singh in 1892, its main building a favourite of film crews. A short stop for the scale and the beauty of the facade, and for the story of Sikh self-assertion under the Raj.

items.name: Gurdwara Baba Deep Singh Shaheedan Sahib
items.description: The shrine marking where the 75-year-old warrior-scholar Baba Deep Singh fell in 1757 defending the desecrated Golden Temple, one of Sikhism's most revered martyrdom sites. A powerful, less-visited stop for those tracing the faith's history of sacrifice.

items.name: Gurdwara Chheharta Sahib
items.description: Built where Guru Arjan Dev sank a great well fed by six Persian wheels, giving the town its name; the sixth Guru was born nearby. A calm, historic gurdwara on the way to the Wagah border, easy to fold into that afternoon.

items.name: Hall Bazaar
items.description: The oldest, busiest market in the city, entered through a Mughal-style gateway, stacked with phulkari, Punjabi juttis, dry fruit and handicrafts. A guide can steer you to the trusted old houses for embroidery and footwear worth carrying home.

items.name: Katra Jaimal Singh Market
items.description: The textile heart of Amritsar, its lanes lined with shops for suits, sarees and wedding fabric at prices that surprise. Punjabi families still come here to buy trousseaux; a knowledgeable escort makes the bargaining painless.

items.name: Papad-Warian Lanes (Majith Mandi)
items.description: The alleys where sun-dried Amritsari papad and spiced lentil warian are made and sold, the smell of asafoetida hanging in the air. A quick, sensory old-city errand that yields the most authentic edible souvenir of Punjab.

items.name: Punjabi Jutti Shopping
items.description: Amritsar's hand-embroidered leather juttis are among the finest in India, made by families who have stitched them for generations. Commissioning a bespoke pair, or fitting the whole family, is a small, memorable indulgence.

items.name: Pul Kanjari
items.description: A little pleasure-stop Maharaja Ranjit Singh built for his dancer Moran, complete with baoli, temple, mosque and gurdwara side by side as a mark of his secular rule. A poignant, near-empty ruin best paired with the Wagah ceremony the same afternoon.

items.name: Gurdwara Tarn Taran Sahib
items.description: Founded by Guru Arjan Dev, this gurdwara holds the largest sarovar of any Sikh shrine, thronged on the monthly Amavas. A serene, grand day-trip that rewards early arrival, well short of the tourist trail.

items.name: Sri Khadoor Sahib
items.description: The home town of the second Guru, Angad Dev, where he formalised the Gurmukhi script and where Mata Khivi ran an early langar. Part of the classic three-gurdwara heritage circuit south of the city, rich in the faith's formative story.

items.name: Gurdwara Baoli Sahib, Goindwal
items.description: The great stepwell of eighty-four steps built by the third Guru, Amar Das, in the 16th century, a place of deep pilgrimage on the banks of the Beas. The furthest and most atmospheric of the day-trip gurdwaras, open from before dawn.

items.name: Pingalwara
items.description: Bhagat Puran Singh's home for the destitute, sick and abandoned, a byword in Punjab for selfless service. A visit, or a quiet contribution, gives a stay a dimension of seva beyond the shrines and the food.

items.name: Saragarhi Memorial Gurdwara
items.description: A memorial to the 21 Sikh soldiers who fought to the last man at Saragarhi in 1897, one of history's most celebrated last stands. Small but stirring, and close enough to the Golden Temple to see in the same morning.

items.name: Sardar Bhagat Singh Museum, Khatkar Kalan
items.description: The ancestral village and museum of the revolutionary Bhagat Singh, preserving his belongings, letters and family home. A longer day-trip for the patriotic and the historically minded, best done with a driver and a picnic.

items.name: Amritsar Food Trail (Guided)
items.description: A curated crawl through the old-city lanes taking in kulcha, lassi, fish tikka, jalebi and kada prasad in a single morning, led by someone who knows every counter. The most delicious way to understand why food is half the reason to come to Amritsar.

items.name: Makhan Fish & Chicken Corner
items.description: For the non-vegetarians, the city's most famous Amritsari fish tikka, batter-fried in the winter season and eaten hot off the tawa. A savoury counterpoint for families who want more than the vegetarian dhaba canon.

items.name: Jalianwala Bagh Light & Sound Show
items.description: The evening projection within the renovated memorial that narrates the 1919 massacre against the bullet-scarred walls. An emotive way to close a day begun at the Golden Temple, and a chance to sit with the history rather than pass through it.

items.name: Golden Temple Roof & Sunset Views
items.description: As the light softens, the gold catches fire and the reflection in the sarovar deepens; the langar hall roof and the parikrama's far side give the calmest vantage. Timing a slow evening circuit for golden hour is the photograph everyone remembers.

items.name: Qila Ahluwalia & The Old City Gates
items.description: Fragments of the fort of the Ahluwalia misl and the surviving gateways of the walled city, woven into the heritage walk, mark the boundary of eighteenth-century Amritsar. Small architectural clues that make the whole old city legible once a guide points them out.

items.name: Makhan Fish & Chicken Corner
credentials: A recognised Amritsar culinary icon (since the 1960s–90s lineage)
Renowned for Amritsari fish (singhara / sohal) and tandoori chicken
items.description: The definitive Amritsari fried fish, crisp, tender singhara fish that made the city's most famous non-veg name.

items.name: Beera Chicken House
credentials: A four-decade Amritsar institution
Renowned for tandoori murga, keema naan and Amritsari fish
items.description: Four decades of smoky tandoori chicken with a dry-rub the city argues over, no colour, no fuss, just fire.

items.name: Surjit Food Plaza
credentials: A long-standing recognised Amritsar restaurant
Renowned for tandoori and Amritsari non-vegetarian classics
items.description: The grand old name of Amritsari non-veg, tandoori meats and fried fish with a fuller sit-down setting.

items.name: Kesar Da Dhaba
items.area: Old City (Chowk Passian, near the Golden Temple)
credentials: Established 1916, a living Amritsar institution
The Better India / Slurrp, favoured by Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Lala Lajpat Rai
Condé Nast Traveller India, Amritsar must-visit
items.description: A century-old pure-vegetarian legend, dal makhani cooked overnight in copper, once served to Nehru and Lala Lajpat Rai.

items.name: Bharawan Da Dhaba
items.area: Old City (near Town Hall / Golden Temple)
credentials: Established 1912, Amritsar's oldest dhaba
YourStory / Slurrp, a century-old Amritsar institution
A ten-minute walk from the Golden Temple
items.description: Amritsar's oldest dhaba, pure-veg Punjabi cooking slow-simmered in desi ghee since a tent in 1912.

items.name: Kanha Sweets
credentials: A landmark Amritsar sweet shop & breakfast institution
Renowned for puri-chole (served 8:30am–3pm)
items.description: The city's morning ritual, puri chole and halwa, plus a sweet counter of pinni, kaju katli and motichoor.

items.name: All India Famous Amritsari Kulcha
credentials: A famed Amritsari kulcha institution
Outlook Traveller, among Amritsar's best kulcha
Praised by chef Vikas Khanna
items.description: The kulcha the city sends you to, crisp, many-layered, butter-soaked, praised by chef Vikas Khanna.

items.name: Gian Chand Lassi Wale (Gian Di Lassi)
credentials: A landmark Hall Bazaar milk bhandar
Renowned for thick peda lassi (makhan, malai, curd)
items.description: A kulhad of peda lassi so rich it doubles as a meal, Hall Bazaar's most famous glass.

items.name: Golden Temple Langar (Guru Ka Langar)
items.area: Old City (within the Golden Temple complex)
credentials: The World Book of Records, world's largest free kitchen
Feeds ~100,000 daily (double on holy days)
Instituted in the 15th–16th century; a UNESCO-recognised living tradition
items.description: The world's largest free kitchen, a simple vegetarian meal served to around 100,000 people a day, to anyone, for free.

items.name: The bar at Taj Swarna
credentials: Inside Taj Swarna, Taj Hotels' Amritsar flagship
items.description: The most composed evening drink in a modest city, Taj service, well-kept spirits and quiet.

items.name: Rooftop cafés overlooking the Golden Temple
credentials: Rooftop cafés on the Golden Temple heritage plaza
The definitive Amritsar evening view, the lit temple after dark
items.description: Not a bar but the city's real night view, chai or a cold coffee above the illuminated temple, mirrored in its pool.

plan.heading: 2 days in Amritsar, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

days.label: Day 1
days.title: The Golden Temple, at its two best hours

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive at Harmandir Sahib soon after dawn, when the marble is cool and the kirtan carries across the sarovar, with a guide who explains the seva rather than rushing you through.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Walk the restored Heritage Street and the Partition Museum at Town Hall, then rest through the afternoon heat.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return to the Golden Temple after dark for the Palki Sahib ceremony, then dinner of Amritsari kulcha and dal at the old-city institution Kesar Da Dhaba.

days.label: Day 2
days.title: The border and the food streets

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A langar visit to see the world's largest community kitchen at work, then the sober, well-told Jallianwala Bagh memorial next door.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Drive out to the Wagah border early enough to be seated properly for the evening Beating Retreat ceremony.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Back in the city for Amritsari fish and kulchas along Lawrence Road, or a quiet dinner at your hotel if the day has been full.

items.name: Heritage Street / near the Golden Temple
items.description: Steps from the temple and the food lanes; best for dawn and night visits on foot.

items.name: Ranjit Avenue
items.description: The newer, calmer part of town with modern hotels; for comfort a short drive from the old city.

items.name: Lawrence Road / Mall area
items.description: Central and lively with dining; suits those wanting a mix of the old and the new.

events.name: Baisakhi
events.note: The Sikh new year and harvest festival, celebrated with great fervour at the Golden Temple; the peak time to witness the faith.

events.name: Guru Nanak Gurpurab
events.note: The birth anniversary of the founder of Sikhism, when the temple is spectacularly illuminated at night.

events.name: Diwali / Bandi Chhor Divas
events.note: The temple and city are lit with lamps and fireworks reflected in the sacred tank; a beautiful night here.

events.name: Lohri
events.note: The Punjabi winter bonfire festival, marked warmly across the city with music and food.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: The Golden Temple asks for covered heads and bare feet, with scarves and a cloakroom provided at the entrance; go at dawn or after dark for the quietest, most luminous darshan, and time the Wagah border ceremony for late afternoon.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Sri Guru Ram Dass Jee International Airport (ATQ), about a 40-minute chauffeured drive to the walled city and the Golden Temple precinct.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver for the city and the Wagah border, and slow walking through the old-city lanes, which are best explored on foot.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Strong Jio and Airtel 4G/5G across the city; a local SIM from the airport is the simplest option.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee; cards are accepted at hotels and larger restaurants, but carry cash for the old bazaars and street food; tipping is modest and appreciated.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: October to March is the window, with 10-25C days ideal for the Golden Temple and Wagah; avoid May-June, when heat nears 40C, and the humid July-August monsoon.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Amritsar (Sri Guru Ram Dass Jee International, ATQ) takes direct flights: Delhi (about 1 hr 15 min), Mumbai (about 2.5 hrs), Bengaluru. Air India and IndiGo fly it in business/premium; for a first-class feel, connect through Delhi's T3 and use the Air India Maharaja lounge before the short hop up.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No special vaccinations beyond routine Hepatitis A/Typhoid. Very safe, welcoming city, even around the temple at night. Stick to bottled or filtered water; the langar food at the Golden Temple is famously clean.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Amritsar is a vegetarian's home ground, from Punjabi thalis to the free langar at the Golden Temple. Jain requests are well understood. Kesar Da Dhaba and Bharawan Da Dhaba are institutions for pure-veg Punjabi cooking.
